content.title: About
content.content: Cheese is a dairy product made by coagulating milk, separating the curds, and pressing them. Hundreds of varieties exist, differing in flavor, texture, and aging time. Cheese is often enjoyed with wine, as the wine’s aromatic compounds highlight the cheese’s taste profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese is produced in more than 150 countries worldwide.
The oldest known cheese dates back to 5500 BC.
There are over 2,000 recognized cheese varieties, from soft to very hard.
Italy has a “cheese trail” tradition, allowing travelers to taste regional cheeses paired with local wines.
Cheese is a staple ingredient in sauces, casseroles, and salads.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese provides a high amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Cheese supplies complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese contains vitamins B2, B12, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Certain aged cheeses contain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Beneficial fatty acids
items.content: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) in cheese may help maintain a healthy weight.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Many cheeses are salty, which can be an issue for those with hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to casein, a protein found in cheese.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese is calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese can be sliced and served as a snack, added to salads, pastas, and casseroles, or paired with fruit and nuts. For wine pairing, choose soft cheeses (e.g., brie) with light white wines and aged hard cheeses (cheddar, parmesan) with dry red wines.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cheese in the refrigerator, wrapped in wax paper or a breathable film to allow it to “breathe.” Hard cheeses keep for several months, soft cheeses for about a week. Before use, check for any mold that is not typical for the variety.

content.title: About
content.content: Cappuccino is a popular coffee drink made of espresso, hot milk, and a thick layer of milk foam. The name comes from the Italian “cappuccino,” referring to the color of the Capuchin monks’ robes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cappuccino first appeared in Italy in the early 1920s.
Traditional cappuccino follows a 1:1:1 ratio of espresso, steamed milk, and foam.
In Japan, iced cappuccino versions served over ice are common.
The foam helps trap aromatic oils from the coffee, enhancing flavor.
Some countries top cappuccino with a dusting of cocoa powder or cinnamon.

items.title: Stimulating effect
items.content: Caffeine in cappuccino stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness and concentration.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine can boost metabolic rate, helping with calorie burning.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee provides vitamins B2 (riboflavin) and B3 (niacin), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: The milk component adds calcium, beneficial for bones and teeth.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine.

items.title: Higher calorie content
items.content: Milk and foam add calories, so portion control is advisable, especially on a diet.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should use lactose‑free or plant‑based milks.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can aggravate gastritis and heartburn in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: For a classic cappuccino, pull a double espresso (30 ml), add an equal amount of steamed milk (≈30 ml), and top with a thick milk foam (≈30 ml). The foam should be dense and creamy; optionally garnish with cocoa or cinnamon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store freshly roasted coffee beans in an airtight container in a cool, dark place for up to 2‑3 weeks. Keep milk refrigerated and use within 5‑7 days. Foam is prepared fresh and should not be stored.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice drink is a beverage made from fresh fruits, enriched with a high amount of vitamin C. It has a light, refreshing taste and is suitable for daily consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vitamin C in the juice helps strengthen the immune system.
The juice retains some of the natural antioxidants from the fruits.
Its light consistency makes it popular among both children and adults.
Often used in cooking as a base for sauces and marinades.
When stored properly, the juice can keep its qualities for up to 7 days.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C protects cells from oxidative stress and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Regular consumption may boost the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The juice is mostly water, helping maintain proper fluid balance.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Fruit polyphenols help combat free radicals.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The juice is quickly absorbed, providing a rapid energy boost.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some fruit juices can have high natural sugar levels, which should be considered for diabetes management.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature may irritate the stomach lining in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Nutrient loss over time
items.content: Prolonged storage can reduce vitamin C levels.

items.title: Allergy to specific fruits
items.content: People allergic to certain fruits should choose juice without those ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled, use it in smoothies, cocktails, or as a base for fruit desserts. It is best to consume freshly prepared juice within 24 hours for maximum vitamin C content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a tightly sealed bottle. For longer storage, use an airtight container and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Michelada is a refreshing Mexican cocktail made with beer, lime juice, Worcestershire sauce, Tabasco sauce, and spices. It is usually served over ice with a salted rim. The drink balances bitter, sour, and mildly spicy flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Originally created in Mexico in the early 20th century as “beer with lemon”.
There are many regional variations that add soy sauce, cucumber juice, or fruit purees.
Traditional serving includes a glass rim coated with salt or lime, often dusted with chili powder.
Michelada is often called a “beer cocktail”; some recipes use light lager, others dark beer.
The drink gained popularity in the United States in the 1990s through Mexican restaurants and bar menus.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Lime and spices provide vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The vinegar and spices can stimulate gastric juice production.

items.title: Quenches thirst
items.content: Salt and acidity help quickly replenish electrolytes after physical activity.

items.title: Contains small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: Beer supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Michelada contains alcohol, so it should be consumed in moderation and avoided during pregnancy, driving, or by children.

items.title: High sodium level
items.content: The salted rim and Worcestershire sauce can increase sodium intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Tabasco and chili powder may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Allergies to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to Worcestershire sauce (contains anchovies) or to beer (gluten).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Michelada in a tall glass over ice, with the rim dipped in lime juice and coated in salt or a salt‑chili mix. Mix beer, lime juice, Worcestershire sauce, Tabasco, and spices, then gently pour into the glass. Garnish with a lime wedge for aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ingredients separately: keep beer in a cool dark place, sauces in the refrigerator after opening. Prepared Michelada is best enjoyed immediately, but if needed it can be refrigerated for up to 24 hours.

rice-white-cooked-with-fat-puerto-rican-.title: Rice, white, cooked with fat, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked with added fat (usually oil or lard) in the Puerto Rican style has a delicate aroma and a slightly buttery texture. Traditionally it is served as a side dish to meat, beans, and vegetable stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Puerto Rican method often starts by sautéing the rice in fat before boiling, giving it a golden hue.
A similar technique is known as "arroz con aceite" in Spain and other Caribbean islands.
Medium‑grain or short‑grain rice is preferred because it absorbs the fat’s flavor better.
Rice is commonly paired with black beans (arroz con gandules) – a classic Puerto Rican combination.
Adding aromatics such as garlic, onion, and cumin enhances the flavor profile.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of carbohydrates that are readily converted into energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: White rice contains thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3), important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies iron and magnesium, supporting blood formation and nerve function.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Cooking with fat makes the rice softer and easier on the stomach.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: Fat slows carbohydrate absorption, helping you feel fuller longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat increases the dish’s calories, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten in excess.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Using butter or lard raises saturated fat levels, which may be undesirable for heart‑health concerns.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, causing rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Allergy to seasonings
items.content: Some recipes include spices or flavorings that could trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side to grilled meat, fish, beans, or vegetable stews. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, cilantro) and a squeeze of lime for brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of water or a little oil to restore softness.

content.title: About
content.content: Saccharin is an artificial sweetener about 300‑400 times sweeter than sugar and contains no calories. The powder form is convenient for precise dosing in cooking, beverages, and pharmaceuticals. It is heat‑stable, making it suitable for baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Saccharin was discovered in 1879 by German chemist Constantin Ferdinand von Fellenberg.
It is one of the first artificial sweeteners to achieve widespread commercial use.
Saccharin is not metabolized by the body, so it does not raise blood glucose levels.
In some countries saccharin intake is limited due to past concerns about carcinogenicity, but modern studies do not confirm a risk.
The powdered form dissolves easily in both cold and hot liquids.

items.title: Supports blood‑sugar control
items.content: Zero calories and carbohydrates make saccharin suitable for people with diabetes or those monitoring glucose.

items.title: Reduces dietary calories
items.content: Replacing sugar with saccharin lowers the energy content of foods without sacrificing sweetness.

items.title: Heat stability
items.content: Saccharin retains its sweetness during baking and cooking, useful for diet‑friendly recipes.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience skin rash or itching when exposed to saccharin.

items.title: Possible gastrointestinal upset
items.content: Large amounts can cause stomach discomfort, bloating, or diarrhea.

items.title: Regulatory limits in some regions
items.content: Certain jurisdictions set maximum acceptable daily intakes (ADIs), so follow manufacturer guidelines.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Powdered saccharin can be added to tea, coffee, smoothies, yogurt, sauces, and dough. For accurate sweetness, use measuring spoons: 1 g of powder is roughly equivalent to 1 tablespoon of sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. Properly stored, it remains good for up to 2 years.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat groats are made from wheat kernels (Triticum) that have been hulled, crushed, or polished. They include Poltava and Artek groats, as well as semolina, bulgur, and couscous. Wheat groats have a mild, neutral flavor. They are cooked as porridge and added to soups, fillings, side dishes, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat is one of the oldest and most widespread cereal crops.
Poltava groats are polished crushed wheat, while Artek groats are finer.
Bulgur is steamed, crushed wheat that cooks very quickly and is popular in the Middle East.
Semolina is finely ground wheat.
Whole-grain groats retain the bran and germ.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Wheat groats provide complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Whole-grain groats, such as bulgur, contain more fiber.

items.title: Contain B vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin, and B6 help the body get energy from food.

items.title: Contain magnesium and manganese
items.content: These minerals support metabolism and muscle function.

items.title: Contain iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and immunity.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat contains gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Wheat allergy can cause reactions of varying severity.

items.title: Bloating
items.content: The fructans and fiber in wheat cause gas in some people.

items.title: Carbohydrates
items.content: Groats are rich in carbohydrates, so people with diabetes should watch their portion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse wheat groats and cook them in water or milk in a ratio of about 1 to 2.5–3 for about 20–30 minutes. Bulgur only needs to be covered with boiling water or cooked for 10–15 minutes. Serve the groats as porridge and a side dish, or add them to soups, fillings, patties, and salads such as tabbouleh.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store groats in an airtight container in a dry, cool, dark place. Whole-grain groats are best kept in the refrigerator, because the fats in the germ can turn rancid. Keep cooked groats in the refrigerator for three to five days.
